ety: From translingual Grandiflora, from New Latin grandiflōra, the feminine form, following the feminine gender of rosa (“rose”), of grandiflōrus (“having large flowers”), from grandis (“large”) + flōs (“flower”, stem flōr-) + -us (suffix forming adjectives; feminine -a).

ety: Borrowed from Latin lōrīca, literally "a corselet of thongs", probably from lorum (“thong”).

senses: One who takes part in, or enjoys watching motor racing.
ety: From rev + -head (“suffix indicating a fan or enthusiast”).
examples: Cars are a religion in Perth, which is still a city of revheads with a bigger membership of car clubs than anywhere else in the country, and Claremont was one of the world′s oldest speedway tracks.
But your seventeen-year-old revhead son would be blown away if you commented on his rims (never call them alloy wheels).
Adelaide′s Crime Stoppers phoneline was pumping: revheads and greenies alike were dobbing in yellow Ford Econovans blowing smoke on the road.

ety: From Middle English gaper, equivalent to gape + -er.

examples: Xenophon, Plato's contemporary, remarks that he finds pitiable those persons who, according to tradition, pour water into a perforated pithos, since they labor in vain.
Only two Hellenistic pithoi in use in the Hellenistic period have been found intact and in situ at the Agora, as far as I am aware.

senses: A gathering for the purpose of singing songs; a musical ceremony.
ety: Borrowed from Hindi संगीत (saṅgīt), from Sanskrit संगीत (saṃgīta), from सम्- (sam-, “together”) + गीत (gīta, “song”).
examples: Justin Bieber landed in Mumbai this week to perform at the couple's sangeet, or musical ceremony, where guests mingled with Indian film and cricket stars.

senses: The study of the purported mystical relationship between numbers (or the letters of words, represented by numbers) and the character or action of physical objects and living beings.
Characterized by flowing water; swiftly flowing; concerned with flowing rivers, streams, etc.
ety: From Latin lotus, past participle of lavare (“to wash”), + -ic.
examples: This particular area is subject to the transition from a more lotic environment to the lentic environment existing in the pool area.
Turning now to more lotic environments, Norelius (1967) and Bronmark and Malmqvist (1982) have studied populations of Anodonta anita and Unio pictorum inhabiting Swedish lake outlets.
Among the main tributaries of the French Rhône River (Arve, Guiers, Ain, Saône, Isère, Eyrieux, Drôme, Ardeche, Durance, Gard), Berahou (1993) considered the lower Ain as one of the most lotic.

senses: The command signal or value which is fed into a controller to establish the target or desired position or state of the controlled device or process.

ety: Inherited from Middle English sighynge. By surface analysis, sigh + -ing.

senses: Somewhat small.
ety: From Middle English smalish, equivalent to small + -ish.
examples: I may say that I'm a married man, living with my wife at that address—a smallish flat which suits us very well as we have no children.

senses: Extenuation; mitigation.
ety: Borrowed from Middle French palliation, from Latin palliare (“to cloak; to conceal”), from Latin pallium (“cloak”). By surface analysis, palliate + -ion.

Alternately increasing and decreasing in severity or intensity.
ety: From Latin remittent-, present participle of remittō.
examples: A remittent fever is when at certain periods the fever is more violent than at others, but the patient never intirely free from it.
The evening was a little chilly, and a fire of logs had been lighted in the study where we were, and the remittent flame and the glow on the walls reminded me of the old days.
